text: Once you have a workspace and know which target you want — simulator, resource estimator, or real hardware — the actual act of running something is the same shape every time: submit a job, poll its status, retrieve its results once it finishes.

Here's that lifecycle from Microsoft's own documentation. Every job, regardless of target, moves through Waiting — queued, not yet started, which is where real-hardware jobs can sit behind other customers' jobs — then Executing, and finally Succeeded or Failed. Submitting a job is never synchronous the way calling a local simulator function is: you get a job handle back immediately, and the actual computation happens somewhere else, on its own schedule.

From the CLI, this is three commands. job submit returns immediately with a job ID once it's accepted into the queue. job show reports its current status. job output retrieves the results once that status is Succeeded. This submit-poll-fetch shape is the same regardless of which target string you pass.

The azure-quantum Python SDK wraps the identical lifecycle into a few calls against your Workspace object. workspace.submit sends the program and gets a job back. wait_until_completed blocks, polling status internally — exactly the loop you'd otherwise write by hand with repeated job-show calls. get_results then returns a histogram of measurement outcomes, once the job has succeeded.

And here's what that looks like for real — a job list straight from the Azure portal: job ID, target, status, submission time, and a cost estimate, all visible before you ever retrieve a result. For a resource-estimator job specifically, the result you'd retrieve here isn't a histogram at all — it's the structured hardware-requirements report from last lesson, so your code needs to know which kind of target produced the job before it tries to interpret the payload.

Three things matter once you're doing this for real. Queueing: real hardware shares a physical device across many customers, so Waiting can last anywhere from seconds to a meaningful while. Cost accrual: real hardware jobs accrue cost per job or per shot, so submitting the same buggy job five times while debugging isn't free. And given both of those, the realistic workflow is dry-run on a simulator first, confirm feasibility with the resource estimator if relevant, and only then submit to real hardware.
That closes out this chapter's Azure Quantum platform work. Chapter 4 puts the whole pipeline to use on real algorithms, starting with Grover's algorithm in Q#.
